analysis.one_liner: Blocks banks from selling your payment and shopping records for marketing unless you opt in.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, the bill died there in March 2001 without a hearing, vote, or cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, the 1999 law that allowed banks, insurers, and securities firms to merge and share data. Under it, a bank could not hand over information about who you write checks to, who you pay, or your marketing and behavioral profiles for the purpose of selling you nonfinancial products unless you got a clear written notice and affirmatively consented in writing. It died in the Senate Banking Committee with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank and credit card customers. Today banks can share or sell records of your payments and shopping behavior for marketing unless you opt out; under this bill the default would flip, and nothing could be shared for marketing nonfinancial products unless you said yes in writing.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits financial institutions from disclosing customer information for marketing nonfinancial products unless the customer is clearly notified and affirmatively consents in writing [S2][S3].
Bars banks from disclosing the identity of anyone a customer paid by check, had a credit transaction with, or received payments from — the raw material of detailed behavioral profiles [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, and data brokers who monetize customer transaction data for cross-marketing would lose that revenue stream, and merchants lose access to the prospective-customer pipelines built on it.

drawbacks.text: Opt-in consent requirements add compliance costs for banks and can cut off consumers from useful offers — people who would have said yes get fewer promotions because they never signed a form [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but narrow: it covers marketing of nonfinancial products and leaves other sharing governed by the weaker opt-out rules of the underlying law. The compliance cost to banks is modest against a clear privacy gain for customers, but the bill never got far enough for anyone to test the trade-off in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Banking Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the bill on March 14, 2001 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day; that is the last action on record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and data brokers kept the ability to share and sell customer payment and behavioral data for marketing under the weaker opt-out regime of Gramm-Leach-Bliley.

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby (R-AL)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over banking privacy law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator sponsored the bill with no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern is on record.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from sharing or selling customer payment and behavioral data for marketing unless the customer opted in, cutting off a revenue stream built on transaction records.
They buy bank-sourced data to build profiles and target consumers; the opt-in requirement would dry up that supply unless each customer consented.
